transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Blake: Ok everyone, thanks for hopping on. We'll run through some of the runtime stuff we promised — hierarchical KV layering, and a lazy kernel-tiling execution path we think helps at 128k and above. Maya will lead the perf bits.
[00:18] Maya Chen: hey, hi. quick context — Stratus said you're seeing heavy tail latency when you hit 80–120k context, and at 128k it spins up long GC like behavior in your workload is that right, Priya?
[00:30] Priya Nair: yeah, correct. we see the tail under load — throughput is okay but a subset of requests go 2–3x latency. also memory pressure because we keep full KV per convo on disk and bring big chunks into RAM.
[00:45] Luis Ortega: and just to add, we're mostly on-prem with a handful of cloud VMs in us-west, so we can't rely on cloud-managed caching. we need options that map to our rack-level NVMe and 8xA100-ish GPU nodes.
[01:02] Maya Chen: perfect, that aligns. so our approach is twofold: first, hierarchical KV layering — small L1 in-GPU KV for hot prefixes, L2 on local NVMe with a compact indexing scheme, and optional L3 remote snapshot bucket for cold history. second, lazy kernel-tiling — we split attention kernel execution into tiled chunks that only materialize KV slices when a tile needs it, avoiding entire-seq matmuls for many time steps.
[01:28] Tom Bishop: when you say "lazy", do you mean you defer KV expansion until the attention window actually intersects? like demand-driven?
[01:36] Maya Chen: exactly, demand-driven. we observed many long prompts have sparse active regions — e.g., instructions plus a long doc that only gets referenced sparsely. so tiling plus a bloom-prefetch for predicted tiles gives big wins.
[01:50] Elena Marcov: is there a quality hit from the bloom-prefetch heuristics? false negatives would increase re-computation.
[01:58] Maya Chen: good question. we tune the bloom filter to favor false positives at the cost of some extra I/O rather than false negatives. in practice for retrieval-like long contexts it matches active tokens >98% and recompute overhead is low.
[02:12] Priya Nair: what about tokenization alignment — our pipelines chunk by paragraphs for embeddings, and we've seen misaligned kv keys. do you have deterministic chunk boundaries?
[02:24] Luis Ortega: also, we use a custom tokenizer variant so we need to verify keying across quantized models.
[02:30] Maya Chen: we recommend canonical chunking at model BPE boundaries with a deterministic rolling hash for keys; for custom tokenizers we provide a shim that normalizes keys. we'll include that in the benchmark repo.
[02:45] Jordan Blake: let's pause — quick architecture note: the runtime supports model-agnostic KV contracts so the layering is independent of model format, but kernel tiling requires cooperating runtimes (we provide a patch for most open models).
[03:00] Tom Bishop: this "patch" — is it a model convert or runtime kernel change?
[03:06] Maya Chen: runtime-level. we compile an alternate attention kernel that accepts tiled inputs and lazyloads kv slices. no model weight changes. so end-to-end model outputs remain the same.
[03:18] Priya Nair: are there constraints for on-prem GPUs? we have multi-tenant nodes and can't OOM other workloads.
[03:26] Luis Ortega: yes, we need per-pod gpu memory cgrouping and strict eviction policies.
[03:30] Luis Ortega: sorry, cgroup, not like "per-pod" in our infra.
[03:32] Maya Chen: we have two mitigations: 1) our runtime exposes per-request working-set caps and will spill tiles to NVMe when thresholds hit; 2) quantization reduces footprint and the lazy tiling reduces peak live KV significantly. together they avoid OOMs in most setups.
[03:48] Jordan Blake: on quantization: we recommend adaptive 8-bit for attention matrices and a mixed q4/8 strategy on MLPs to balance quality vs perf. Maya?
[03:56] Maya Chen: yeah — our internal evals showed for instruction-following tasks that a Q4_0-like path on MLPs keeps quality within ~1–2% on rouge/bertscore while giving 2.5–3x memory reduction. but you must calibrate per-model. for retrieval-heavy workloads, aggressive quant can slightly degrade reranking precision.
[04:18] Elena Marcov: how transparent is calibration? we need to run tests against our evaluation sets.
[04:22] Maya Chen: we'll deliver quant profiles plus an adaptive calibration harness — it runs eval sets with a blind rollback if quality regresses beyond a threshold. we'll include scripts.
[04:32] Priya Nair: okay good. now about latency — if we tile, do we introduce extra kernel launch overheads that hurt p50?
[04:40] Maya Chen: micro-benchmarks show kernel launch adds ~0.6-1.2 ms per tile depending on GPU and driver. but because each tile is smaller, it fits L2C caches better and reduces expensive memory copies, net p50 is usually flat or slightly improved; p95/p99 improves because we avoid huge matmuls that block.
[04:58] Tom Bishop: curious about batching. we typically batch at the request layer to amortize token compute. does tiling play nice with batching?
[05:06] Maya Chen: yes — we do "tile-aligned batching." we merge tiles across requests when they address the same token ranges; batching policies are workload-aware so latency SLOs are preserved for high-priority routes.
[05:18] Priya Nair: any special NVMe config suggestions? our nodes have consumer NVMe and a small enterprise pool.
[05:24] Luis Ortega: and we want predictable IO — not garbage.
[05:28] Maya Chen: prefer NVMe with stable 99th percentile IOPS; we rely on async IO with prefetch queues. for durability, L2 writes are append-only with periodic compaction. avoid consumer drives with aggressive power management. we'll document recommended fio profiles.
[05:42] Elena Marcov: network encryption for L3 snapshots — we need to ensure HSM keys and per-tenant KMS integration.
[05:48] Jordan Blake: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and we ship an integration guide. for air-gapped we have an on-prem bundle that includes an offline attestation flow.
[05:58] Priya Nair: do you integrate with HashiCorp Vault or cloud KMS?
[06:02] Asha Patel: yes — Vault, AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure, and we support HSMs via PKCS#11 for on-prem. Asha will share the integration matrix.
[06:10] Tom Bishop: back to perf — what's the rough throughput delta for 128k vs 256k using tiling + KV layering vs naive full-kv? ballpark numbers are fine.
[06:20] Maya Chen: naive full-kv at 128k has per-token marginal cost that scales roughly O(n) due to attention matmul and memory pressure. our tiling+layering reduces per-token effective cost — in our tests at 128k we saw 2.2x improvement in tokens/sec and p99 latency down by ~45%. at 256k it's more pronounced: 3–3.5x tokens/sec improvement and p99 down by ~60% in workloads with sparse access.
[06:51] Elena Marcov: wow. any cases where it regresses? dense cross-attention where the model references most of history?
[06:58] Maya Chen: yes, in dense workloads you won't see the same wins; tiling then just adds overhead, so we detect density and fall back to a dense execution path. runtime does automatic mode selection.
[07:10] Priya Nair: can we force fallback manually? we might want to for deterministic reproducibility.
[07:14] Luis Ortega: and for debugging.
[07:16] Maya Chen: absolutely — runtime exposes both auto and manual modes via config flags and per-route control.
[07:22] Jordan Blake: quick interruption — question from Tom: how does this interact with checkpointing for long-lived KV?
[07:27] Maya Chen: we snapshot compacted L2 indices and support incremental checkpoints — checkpointing frequency is tunable. in on-prem we recommend nightly compaction and hourly snapshots for active sessions.
[07:38] Tom Bishop: sounds reasonable. on the security side, audit logs for KV access — we need immutable logs and per-token access traces for compliance.
[07:46] Asha Patel: our access logs can be shipped to your SIEM; per-request token metadata is recorded but we avoid storing plaintext user content unless configured. we can integrate with your log retention policies.
[07:58] Priya Nair: what's the latency of KV L2 retrieval from NVMe compared to JIT prefetching?
[08:04] Maya Chen: NVMe read p99 in our testnet is ~1.5–3ms per tile depending on size. prefetch amortizes that so most misses never hit critical path. if you get a cold miss you may see a 5–15ms hiccup depending on network and compaction.
[08:20] Jordan Blake: I'm going to jump to planned bench runs — Maya, propose the test matrix?
[08:24] Maya Chen: sure. baseline: 1) Naive full-kv run at 64k, 128k; 2) Tiling+KV layering at 64k, 128k, 256k; 3) Quant profiles: full FP16, adaptive int8, mixed q4/q8. Each with 10k request synthetic trace (mix of dense and sparse). We'll output p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, GPU mem, NVMe IO.
[08:45] Tom Bishop: can we include a real sample of our workload — long-form analyst notes plus periodic retrievals?
[08:52] Maya Chen: yes, please share a sanitized sample; we'll replicate tokenization.
[08:56] Priya Nair: on the topic of quant and MLPs — our legal team is worried about non-determinism from quantized inference for auditability. can you produce bit-for-bit reproducibility?
[09:06] Maya Chen: quantization and parallel execution preclude bit-for-bit reproducibility across runs in many cases. we provide deterministic modes that serialize execution (at cost) and a signed result hash pipeline for audit trails; we'll include options in the runbook.
[09:20] Elena Marcov: curious about debugging — stack traces when a tile fails, does the runtime map back to token offsets?
[09:25] Luis Ortega: and how verbose are the logs? we don't want huge log churn.
[09:28] Maya Chen: runtime maps faults to token ranges and provides a compact error blob with offsets. logs are configurable to sample at different rates to control volume.
[09:36] Jordan Blake: ok, next: VPC/on-prem deployment model and pricing note — Jordan explains commercial options briefly.
[09:42] Jordan Blake: we have three modes: Hosted API, Dedicated reserved pools, and Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem). For Stratus' constraints we recommend Redwood Private with customer-managed KMS and optional reserved capacity for predictable SLAs. Pricing: rough ranges will be in the doc; we'll provide exact quotes after basic sizing run.
[09:58] Priya Nair: what SLAs do you offer for on-prem installs?
[10:02] Jordan Blake: SLA for Dedicated includes uptime SLAs and latency SLOs; for Private we offer an enterprise support add-on with targeted P50/P95 guidance and runbook support. specifics depend on commitment term. we'll include the enterprise pack outline.
[10:14] Tom Bishop: one last deep question — when you do spill to NVMe, do you ever degrade to CPU-bound decryption if using HSM per-request?
[10:22] Asha Patel: HSM operations are off the hot path; keys are wrapped and cached securely in memory with TTLs. per-request decryption from HSM is rare; we use HSM for key unwrap and ephemeral keys thereafter to avoid CPU-bound limitations.
[10:36] Priya Nair: great. any gotchas we should know about for on-prem network topology?
[10:40] Maya Chen: network latency between GPU nodes and NVMe racks should be <200us ideally. avoid oversubscribed top-of-rack switches for active partitions. also, MTU and RDMA options can help for very tight p50 budgets.
[10:55] Tom Bishop: oh and driver versions?
[10:57] Luis Ortega: our ops team hates driver churn.
[11:00] Maya Chen: we publish tested driver/kernel matrices; we'll include a recommended bundle. we also provide a container image for the runtime to limit host dependencies.
[11:09] Jordan Blake: wrapping — agreed next steps and recapping actions.
[11:13] Priya Nair: quick note: we'll try to provision the VPC test account by Monday.
[11:16] Jordan Blake: thanks — Maya will send the perf harness and scripts, Asha the security pack, I'll follow up with pricing.
[11:22] Elena Marcov: thanks all, this was useful.
[11:25] Jordan Blake: thanks, everyone. end.

Notes: shared links mentioned during the call — /redwood/docs/long-context-kv-layering (awaiting access), perf repo (link to be shared), security pack (will be emailed). Some transcription artifacts: "kernel-tiling" heard as "kernel timing" at times, "KV" sometimes transcribed as "K V".
